summary: Specifies a new certificate type and two TLS extensions that let TLS and DTLS peers exchange raw public keys for authentication, without a full certificate.

eli5.summary: Normally you show an ID card from an office. Here you just show your key itself, and the other side already knows to trust that key.

questions: what is a raw public key in tls
how does tls use raw public keys
subtitle: Let TLS and DTLS peers authenticate with a bare public key instead of a full certificate.

tldr.problem: TLS normally ships public keys inside PKIX certificates checked against a certification authority, which is complex, large and wasteful when the certificate is self-signed or its other fields are never used.
tldr.mechanism: A new certificate type, RawPublicKey, carries just the SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure. Two hello extensions, client_certificate_type and server_certificate_type, let each side negotiate which certificate types to use.
tldr.outcome: Keys are smaller and the code simpler, but authentication only works if the key is bound to its owner by some out-of-band method.

today: RFC 7250 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Raw Public Keys
sections.content:
TLS usually obtains client and server public keys in PKIX containers during the handshake, validated against trust anchors from a certification authority. The RFC notes that this can add a complicated trust relationship that is hard to validate. Smaller deployments often use self-signed certificates distributed out of band, which still means generating a certificate whose contents are never used.

The RFC lists other ways to learn a peer's key: DNSSEC-secured records through DANE, a certificate chain fetched from an LDAP server or web page, or keys provisioned into a device image. An example is a smart object using CoAP over DTLS that is configured during manufacturing with the address and public key of its server and its own key pair.

A raw public key keeps only the SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure from a PKIX certificate. That makes it small and needs only a minimalistic ASN.1 parser, with no certificate path validation code.
sections.eli5: A full certificate is like a big folder of papers when all you need is one page. Sending just that page is quicker and needs less work to read.

sections.title: The Raw Public Key Structure
sections.content:
The Certificate payload of the handshake is reused as a container. When the certificate type is RawPublicKey, it holds an opaque ASN.1_subjectPublicKeyInfo; for X.509 it holds the usual certificate list.

The SubjectPublicKeyInfo is defined in Section 4.1 of RFC 5280. It contains an algorithm identifier, which can include parameters, and the key bits. The value in the Certificate payload MUST be the DER encoding of the structure. The RFC gives example algorithm OIDs for RSA, DSA and ECDSA, and notes the list is not exhaustive.

Appendix A shows a worked example: a SEQUENCE holding an rsaEncryption OID and a BIT STRING with a 1024 bit integer and the exponent 65537.
sections.eli5: The key travels in the same envelope a certificate would use. Inside is a short card that names the kind of lock and shows its shape.

sections.title: Negotiating Certificate Types
sections.content:
Two new extensions are added to the hellos: client_certificate_type and server_certificate_type. No new cipher suites are needed; any suite whose key exchange is compatible can be used. No other TLS message is changed.

In the client hello each extension carries a list of supported types sorted by client preference. The first says what the client can send if asked for a certificate. The second says what the client can process from the server. A client MUST leave out types it cannot use, and if only the default X.509 type remains it MUST omit the extension.

The server may ignore the extensions, or, if it supports them but shares no type with the client, end the session with a fatal unsupported_certificate alert. Otherwise, in the server hello, server_certificate_type states the single type it puts in its Certificate payload. To request a client certificate, the server MUST include client_certificate_type, chosen from the client's list, together with a certificate_request.
sections.eli5: Before showing IDs, each side says which kinds it can handle. The server picks one that works for both, and if there is none they stop.

sections.title: Example Handshakes
sections.content:
The RFC gives three exchanges. In the first only the server uses a raw public key: the client lists RawPublicKey in server_certificate_type and omits the client extension, and the server replies with that type and a raw key in its Certificate payload. The client then checks the key by an out-of-band technique such as DANE.

In the second, both sides use raw public keys, which the RFC describes as a use case for smart object networking. The server includes a certificate_request and a client_certificate_type of RawPublicKey.

The third mixes types. The client offers RawPublicKey, X.509 and OpenPGP for the server, preferring raw keys by listing them first, and offers a raw key for itself. The server answers with an X.509 certificate and still asks the client for a raw public key.
sections.eli5: The examples show three cases: only the server shows a key, both show keys, or the server shows a full ID while the client shows just a key.

sections.title: Binding Keys to Identities
sections.content:
Raw keys lower the over-the-air overhead and simplify parsing code. The main security challenge is tying the key to a specific entity. Without a secure binding between identifier and key, the protocol is open to man-in-the-middle attacks. Authentication of client or server is supported only through an out-of-band method, and specifications that use the extensions need to say how that binding is done, and implementations need to check its status.

DANE authenticates keys through DNSSEC. Pre-configured keys are another option; the RFC says they are not suitable for generic Web e-commerce but are reasonable for many smart object deployments. The approach must be chosen before deployment.

An attacker could try to alter the handshake so the parties pick different certificate types. Doing so changes the handshake message hashes, so the Finished messages fail, and without the master_secret the attacker cannot repair them.
sections.eli5: A bare key proves nothing alone. You must already know, from some other trusted place, whose key it is.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered value 2 with description Raw Public Key in the TLS Certificate Types subregistry. It also allocated the two extension types, client_certificate_type and server_certificate_type, from the TLS ExtensionType Values subregistry. They are used in both client hello and server hello, and their values come from the Certificate Types subregistry.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers got new entries so that everyone uses the same number for raw keys.

messages.label: client_hello + server_certificate_type=(RawPublicKey)
messages.note: Client says it can process a raw key.
